newsitem.title: UK: Sweden's Sydkraft to move to high sulphur fuel.
newsitem.headline: Sweden's Sydkraft to move to high sulphur fuel.

text.p: Upgrading work at a 900 megawatt power plant owned by a Swedish private utility will boost imports of high sulphur fuel oil while cutting those of low sulphur fuel, a source at the company said on Thursday.

A new scrubbing unit is expected to be operational at one of three 300 MW units at Sydkraft's Karlshamm plant in southeastern Sweden in November, which will enable it to buy fuel oil with a far higher sulphur content.
"We expect to buy between zero and a maximum of 50,000 tonnes of high sulphur fuel oil per month," the source said.
The new cargoes will need to be of a maximum density of 0.965 kg per litre, which excludes a large number of non-Russian cargoes which are usually sold in northwest Europe.
European traders said the company had already started buying these cargoes on the European spot market to build up their stocks ahead of the changeover.
One cargo of Russian M-100 high sulphur fuel oil was heard sold to Sydcraft earlier this week, and traders said on Thursday they still saw the utility as a buyer in coming weeks.
The oil-fired plant is marginal to the common power grid shared by Nordic countries and is used in times of low hydroelectric output.
Sydkraft has in previous years burned between 50,000 and 400,000 tonnes of low sulphur fuel oil per year, depending on water levels in the region.
Nordic countries' tight environmental legislation places strict limits on the sulphur content of fuel that is burned.
Sydcraft currently burns product containing a maximum of around 0.3 to 0.4 percent sulphur, compared to regular purchases by various U.K. utilities containing three percent sulphur or more.
Very low sulphur fuel oil cargoes are hard to find -- one recent Sydkraft purchase was sourced out of Indonesia.

The source said he thought his company's total fuel oil purchases would rise as a result of the new scrubbing unit because high sulphur cargoes are cheaper than low sulphur ones, and the scrubber would enable the plant's total sulphur emissions to fall more easily within the legal limits.
But he declined to predict trends or speculate on the precise ratio of levels of high sulphur to low sulphur in future purchases.
High sulphur cracked fuel oil carges delivered in northwest Europe are currenly worth around $107 a tonne.
Low sulphur cargoes with a maximum of one percent sulphur are worth around $10 a tonne more.
